pages.text: A political party is a group that helps candidates run in elections and take part in government. Most countries have political parties. They are a big part of politics in both democracies and autocracies today.
pages.caption: In A Block for the Wigs (1783), James Gillray caricatured Fox's return to power in a coalition with North. George III is the blockhead in the centre.

pages.text: Parties can grow out of existing divisions in society, such as differences between lower and upper classes. They help make political decisions easier by encouraging members to cooperate and work together toward common goals.
pages.caption: It is easier for voters to evaluate one simple list of policies for each party, like this platform for the United Australia Party, than to individually judge every single candidate.

pages.text: Many political parties are motivated by specific ideas. Democratic elections often feature liberal, conservative, and socialist parties. Other parties focus on different goals, or they may be formed mainly to help a specific leader.

pages.text: The idea of people forming large groups to share their interests is very ancient. However, modern political parties are considered to have first appeared around the end of the eighteenth century in Europe and America.
pages.caption: Parties can arise from existing cleavages in society, like the Social Democratic Party of Germany which was formed to represent German workers.

pages.text: Political parties usually have a single leader, a group of executives who perform administrative tasks, and everyday members. Citizens can volunteer, give money, and vote for the candidates who represent their party.

B1-B2.headline: The History and Structure of Parties

pages.text: A political party is an organization that coordinates candidates to compete in elections and participate in governance. Party members often hold similar ideas about politics and promote specific ideological or policy goals in many countries around the world.

pages.text: Political parties can develop from existing social divisions, streamlining the process of decision-making. They typically include a party leader, administrative executives, and regular members who volunteer, donate money, and vote for the candidates.

pages.text: Although ancient factions existed in Classical Athens and the Roman Republic, modern political parties emerged around the end of the eighteenth century in Europe and the United States, with several early British groups setting important precedents.

pages.text: Political scientists have proposed several explanations for why parties are ubiquitous. Parties arise from social cleavages, provide compatible incentives for candidates to cooperate, and serve as cognitive heuristics that reduce the burden of voting.

C1-C2.headline: Origins and Functions of Political Parties

pages.text: Political parties are collective entities that organize competitions for political offices and participate in governance. They represent a nearly ubiquitous feature of modern states, operating across both democratic systems and single-party autocracies alike.
pages.caption: In A Block for the Wigs (1783), James Gillray caricatured Fox's return to power in a coalition with North. George III is the blockhead in the centre.

pages.text: The genesis of parties is frequently attributed to pre-existing social cleavages, though critics argue this theory obscures the reciprocal effect wherein parties actively reshape those underlying social divisions.

pages.text: Beyond social divisions, institutional explanations emphasize how party structures generate compatible incentives. These arrangements prevent politicians from acting to each other's detriment during campaigns or governance, which ensures long-term electoral competitiveness against unaffiliated politicians.

pages.text: Psychologically, political parties function as simplifying heuristics. They mitigate the cognitive burden on electors by allowing them to evaluate overarching platforms and party slates rather than numerous independent candidates individually, although some evidence indicates that the strength of party identification has been weakening over recent decades.

pages.text: Structurally, political parties typically comprise a party leader, administrative executives who manage organizational and administrative tasks, and party members. While democratic parties usually select leadership through open and competitive methods, autocratic parties exercise tight control. Furthermore, many countries legally define requirements for an organization to qualify as a political party.
